prompt: our biggest client buys about 800 licences a year at 120 each and wants 4% off every licence if they add 100 more next year. what should i counter with?
rubric: Works out what the 4% across all 900 licences costs against what the extra 100 bring: roughly 3,840 given up on the existing 800, so the 100 new licences net about 7,680, around 77 each against a list of 120.
Says plainly that the offer is really a deep discount on the new licences paid for by cutting the price of the ones they already buy, rather than treating 4% as small.

Proposes a concrete counter that ties the discount to the added volume (for example a lower price only on the extra licences, or a step that applies once they actually reach 900) instead of a blanket cut on the base.
Asks for something in return or sets a condition, such as a commitment to the 900 for the year, a longer term, or payment terms, rather than giving the discount for a promise of intent.
Gives a number or range to open with and a floor to hold, not only general principles.

prompt: we're raising prices 7% in march. our two largest accounts each pay about 70k a year after their usual 30% volume discount. they say they'll only accept the rise if the 30% applies to the increase too, so they'd pay 4.9% more instead of 7%. how do we handle it?
rubric: Sizes the gap in money: about 4,900 versus 3,430 on a 70k bill, roughly 1,470 a year per account, and notes this is small next to the roughly 30k a year each already given up through the discount.
Points out that the real question is whether the 30% discount is still earned by the volume these accounts bring, not the 2.1 percentage points of the rise.
Suggests a trade rather than a free concession: for example accept the 4.9% in exchange for a longer term, a volume commitment, or earlier payment, or hold the 7% and offer something non-price.

Warns that a one-off exception for the two accounts can become the expectation at every future rise, and recommends stating a rule (what the discount applies to) so it is applied the same way next time.
Gives a clear recommended response and a way to say it to the two accounts, not just a list of options.

prompt: we missed delivery dates twice for a client this year. they pay us about 240k a year and now want a permanent 10% cut to their rate. what should we offer instead?
rubric: States what the request costs over time: 24k a year, every year, for a problem that happened twice and may be fixed.
Separates paying for the failure from changing the price, and offers a one-off or time-limited remedy (a credit, a free month, a fee refund on the late jobs) sized to the harm done.
Proposes a service commitment with a measurable target and a credit that applies only if it is missed again, so any lasting reduction is earned by performance rather than granted up front.
Recommends fixing and showing the cause (what changed in delivery), since price alone does not repair the loss of trust.
Recognises the account is large and worth keeping, so the answer is a real offer with numbers, not a flat refusal.

prompt: every quarter end our sales team gives 15 to 20% off to close, and customers have started waiting for it. how do we stop without wrecking this quarter?
rubric: Names the cause: buyers have learned that waiting is rewarded, so the discount now buys timing rather than extra business, and the pattern will persist while it works.

Recommends changes that bite without a hard stop on day one: for example a firm cap on discounts at quarter end, requiring something in return (longer term, bigger commitment, prepayment), and an expiry date on every offer.
Suggests changing how reps are rewarded or approvals are checked (for example commission on net price, or manager sign-off above a lower limit) since incentives drive the habit.
Addresses this quarter specifically: what to do with deals already waiting for a discount, such as holding a smaller discount for those that give something back, and accepting that some slip.
Suggests measuring the effect (share of deals discounted, average discount, deals closed in the last two weeks versus earlier) so the team can see whether it is working.

prompt: how would i check whether our discounts actually make sense? we have invoice data for about 300 business accounts, including rebates and free months.
rubric: Starts by turning each account into one comparable net price per unit after all rebates, credits and free months, rather than comparing headline discount percentages.
Compares net price against what the account gives us (volume, term length, payment terms, growth), for example by grouping similar-sized accounts and looking at the spread within each group.

Looks for the patterns that signal trouble: accounts paying much less than others of the same size and type with no stated reason, discounts stacked on top of one another, and discounts that never expire.

Cuts the data by who granted it and when (rep, quarter-end, approval level) to see whether discounting follows judgment or habit, and says to check what happened to the large-discount accounts afterwards (did they grow or stay).
Ends with what to do with findings: a short list of outliers to review first, and a rule or record of reasons for new discounts, rather than just an analysis plan.

prompt: reps can approve up to 10% off, managers up to 20%, and anything above goes to the vp. deals are stalling while they wait for sign-off and the sales director wants to raise the rep limit to 25% so they can move faster. is that the right fix?
rubric: Questions whether the slow sign-off is really the problem and separates two fixes: making approvals faster (a same-day response target, a clear request form) versus giving away more authority.
Warns that raising the rep limit to 25% will move the whole distribution of discounts upward and that many requests will cluster just under whatever the new limit is.
Suggests looking at the data first: how many requests are over 10%, how long they wait, and how many of the approved ones were actually needed to win.
Offers a middle path that links authority to what the customer gives (for example higher rep limits only for longer terms or larger commitments), rather than a flat percentage ceiling.
Gives a clear recommendation, not only a list of considerations.

prompt: we're bidding on a 3-year tender to support a council's laptops. our normal rate has about 30% margin. the scoring is 60% price and 40% quality and we plan to bid 18% under our rate card to be sure we win, with the price fixed for all three years. does that plan hold up?
rubric: Works out what is left: an 18% cut takes a 30% margin to roughly 12 on 82, about 15% of the price, meaning profit per unit falls by around 60%, and that a fixed price for three years leaves nothing for cost rises.
Asks how the price score is calculated (relative to the lowest bid, a formula, a cap), because 'to be sure we win' may be spending far more margin than needed or not enough to win.
Points out that a lower price is only worth bidding if the scope is fixed, and asks what volume, response times and extras the spec leaves open that could make the work cost more than assumed.

Suggests protecting the margin by other means: an indexation or review clause for the three years, pricing the optional extras separately, and a walk-away price below which the bid is not worth winning.
Takes a position on whether to proceed and at what level, rather than only listing risks.

prompt: a bakery that orders from us every week asked for 5% off if they pay for the whole year upfront. that seems fine to me. anything i'm missing?
rubric: Agrees that this is a reasonable trade and says to accept it (possibly with a brief confirmation of terms), without turning it into a pricing project.
Mentions only the few practical checks that matter, such as what happens to the prepaid balance if prices change or they stop ordering, and writing the terms down.
Does not invent risks, demand a full audit, insist on an approval process, or push a complicated counter-offer for what is a small, fair discount.
Keeps the answer short.

prompt: the buyer asked if we can do 3% off for paying the full year upfront. we're happy to. write me a short reply.
rubric: Is a short reply, a few sentences at most, that says yes to the 3% off for payment of the full year upfront.

States the terms clearly enough to avoid later disputes: that the discount applies to the annual total, that payment is due up front or by a stated date, and what the 3% comes to if a figure was supplied, without inventing amounts.
Does not add extra concessions, a negotiation, a counter-offer or a lecture about discounting.
Reads as a normal, friendly business email with a clear next step (such as sending the invoice).

prompt: we give registered charities 10% off list on all our plans. they send us their charity number and we apply it at checkout. any problem with that?
rubric: Treats this as a normal, sound segment discount: it has a clear rule, a verifiable condition and a fixed amount, and says so.
Mentions only light-touch points, such as checking the number is valid and the discount does not stack with other offers.
Does not recommend dropping the discount, building an approval process, or negotiating terms in return, which would be over-engineering for a published rule.
Keeps the answer proportionate and short.
